title: Joins
summary: Inner joins that silently drop rows, GroupJoin and the left-join pattern, and dictionaries and lookups for fast matching.

steps.title: Join is an inner join
body: You met `Join` in module 6. Two facts about it cause most join bugs:
1. An item with **no partner is dropped**, on both sides.
2. An item with **several partners appears several times**, once per pair.
c => c.Id,                 // key from the left
o => o.CustomerId,         // key from the right
The same in query syntax. Note the keyword is `equals`, not `==`, and the left key must come first:
var q = from c in customers
join o in orders on c.Id equals o.CustomerId

steps.prompt: Omar has no orders and order `9` has no customer. What does this print?
code: var customers = new[] { new Customer(1, "Maya"), new Customer(2, "Omar"), new Customer(3, "Lena") };
var orders = new[] { new Order(1, 30m), new Order(1, 45m), new Order(3, 15m), new Order(9, 99m) };
var q = customers.Join(orders, c => c.Id, o => o.CustomerId, (c, o) => $"{c.Name}:{o.Total}");
steps.explain: Maya has two orders, so she appears twice. Omar (no orders) and order 9 (no customer) are silently dropped. No error, just missing rows: check your counts after a join.

steps.title: GroupJoin: every left item, with its matches
body: Often you want **every** customer, each with **their list** of orders, even if that list is empty. That is `GroupJoin`:
The result selector gets one customer and a **sequence** of their orders. Every customer appears exactly once.
In query syntax it is `join ... into`:
join o in orders on c.Id equals o.CustomerId into theirs

steps.prompt: Using the same data (Omar has no orders), what does `GroupJoin` give for Omar?
steps.code: customers.GroupJoin(orders, c => c.Id, o => o.CustomerId, (c, theirs) => (c.Name, theirs))
options: No result: Omar is dropped like in `Join`
It throws, because Omar has no match
steps.explain: That is the whole point of `GroupJoin`: one result per left item, and an unmatched one gets an **empty** sequence, never `null`. So `Count()` and `Sum()` on it are safe.

steps.title: The left join pattern
body: SQL's `LEFT JOIN` gives one **row per pair**, plus one row with blanks for each left item that had no match. LINQ builds it from three pieces:
var rows = from c in customers
join o in orders on c.Id equals o.CustomerId into theirs
from x in theirs.DefaultIfEmpty()        // empty group -> one null
2. `DefaultIfEmpty()` turns an **empty** group into a group holding one `default` (here `null`).
Because `x` can be `null`, use `?.` and `??` when you read it.

steps.prompt: Complete the left join so that Omar shows up as `Omar: 0`.
code: var rows = from c in customers
join o in orders on c.Id __1__ o.CustomerId __2__ theirs
steps.explain: `equals` compares the keys, `into` keeps the groups (a GroupJoin), and `DefaultIfEmpty` gives an empty group one `null` item so the customer survives the final `from`.

steps.title: Matching fast: dictionaries and lookups
body: The obvious way to match two lists is a loop inside a loop, which checks **every pair**. With 10,000 orders and 10,000 customers that is 100 million comparisons.
foreach (var c in customers)          // slow: scans all customers for every order
`Join` does not do that. It builds a hash table of one side first, then looks each item up. You can do the same by hand, which is handy when you match **many times**:
var customerById = customers.ToDictionary(c => c.Id);   // one per key
var ordersByCustomer = orders.ToLookup(o => o.CustomerId); // many per key
customerById[7]            // throws if 7 is missing; use TryGetValue
ordersByCustomer[7]        // empty sequence if 7 is missing, never throws
Build it **once**, outside any loop, then each lookup is instant.

code: var orders = new[] { new Order(1, 30m), new Order(1, 45m), new Order(3, 15m) };
steps.explain: A lookup with a missing key gives an empty sequence, so `Count()` is 0. `byCustomer.Count` is the number of **keys** (1 and 3). `ToDictionary` throws because customer 1 has two orders and a dictionary key must be unique.

steps.title: Staff directory
prompt: Write `static List<string> Directory(List<Employee> staff, List<Department> depts)` with a join (`Join` or `join ... on ... equals`). One line per employee whose department exists, as `"Ana (Sales)"`, sorted by employee name. Employees with an unknown `DeptId` are left out.
starter: static List<string> Directory(List<Employee> staff, List<Department> depts)
solution: static List<string> Directory(List<Employee> staff, List<Department> depts)
.Join(depts, e => e.DeptId, d => d.Id, (e, d) => new { e.Name, Dept = d.Name })
template: var dojoDepts = new List<Department> { new(1, "Sales"), new(2, "IT"), new(3, "Legal") };
var dojoStaff = new List<Employee> { new("Omar", 2), new("Ana", 1), new("Zed", 9), new("Cy", 1) };
Dojo.Eq("joined and sorted, unknown department left out", new List<string> { "Ana (Sales)", "Cy (Sales)", "Omar (IT)" }, Directory(dojoStaff, dojoDepts));
Dojo.Eq("no departments means nobody", new List<string>(), Directory(dojoStaff, new List<Department>()));
hints: Keep both names in an anonymous object, sort by the employee name, then format.
An inner join drops `Zed` for you: that is exactly what the task wants.

steps.title: Every customer, even the quiet ones
prompt: Write `static List<string> CustomerTotals(List<Customer> customers, List<Order> orders)`. One line for **every** customer, in the order of `customers`, as `"Maya: 2 orders, 75"`. A customer with no orders is `"Omar: 0 orders, 0"`. No loops.
starter: static List<string> CustomerTotals(List<Customer> customers, List<Order> orders)
solution: static List<string> CustomerTotals(List<Customer> customers, List<Order> orders)
template: var dojoCustomers = new List<Customer> { new(1, "Maya"), new(2, "Omar"), new(3, "Lena") };
var dojoOrders = new List<Order> { new(1, 30m), new(3, 15m), new(1, 45m), new(8, 5m) };
Dojo.Eq("every customer once, with counts and totals", new List<string> { "Maya: 2 orders, 75", "Omar: 0 orders, 0", "Lena: 1 orders, 15" }, CustomerTotals(dojoCustomers, dojoOrders));
Dojo.Eq("no orders at all", new List<string> { "Maya: 0 orders, 0", "Omar: 0 orders, 0", "Lena: 0 orders, 0" }, CustomerTotals(dojoCustomers, new List<Order>()));
hints: `Join` would drop Omar. You want every customer exactly once.
`GroupJoin` hands the result selector a customer and the sequence of their orders.

steps.title: Who reports to whom
prompt: The tests define `record Staff(int Id, string Name, int? ManagerId);`

Write `static List<string> WithManagers(List<Staff> staff)`: one line per person, in list order, as `"Bo -> Ana"`. If `ManagerId` is `null` or not the id of anyone in the list, write `"Ana -> (none)"`.
The list can be long, so do **not** search the whole list for every person. Build a `Dictionary` from id to name **once** with `ToDictionary`, then look each manager up.
starter: // slow version: searches every person for every person
solution: var nameById = staff.ToDictionary(s => s.Id, s => s.Name);
.Select(s => $"{s.Name} -> {(s.ManagerId is int id && nameById.TryGetValue(id, out var boss) ? boss : "(none)")}")
template: var dojoStaff = new List<Staff> { new(1, "Ana", null), new(2, "Bo", 1), new(3, "Cy", 2), new(4, "Di", 99) };
Dojo.Eq("managers looked up", new List<string> { "Ana -> (none)", "Bo -> Ana", "Cy -> Bo", "Di -> (none)" }, WithManagers(dojoStaff));
Dojo.Eq("an empty list", new List<string>(), WithManagers(new List<Staff>()));
record Staff(int Id, string Name, int? ManagerId);

forbid.message: Does not search the list for each person

hints: `var nameById = staff.ToDictionary(s => s.Id, s => s.Name);` before the query.
`ManagerId` is an `int?`. `s.ManagerId is int id` checks for null and unwraps in one go.

steps.title: Sidekick: the invoice
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** `sk invoice` bills your logged time per project. Write it with two joins and no loops.
`static List<string> InvoiceLines(IEnumerable<TaskItem> tasks, IEnumerable<TimeEntry> entries, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, decimal> hourlyRates)`
1. **Inner join** entries to tasks on `TaskId == Id` (an entry whose task is gone is not billed), and add up the minutes per project. A task with no `Project` counts as `"(no project)"`.
2. **Left join** those totals to `hourlyRates` on the project name, so a project with no rate still shows up.

3. Sorted by project name. Each line: the project padded to 14 (`{p,-14}`), a space, `Sk.FormatMinutes(minutes)` right-aligned in 8 (`{x,8}`), two spaces, then either the amount `minutes / 60m * rate` as `{amount,10:0.00}` or the text `unbilled (no rate)`:

Given in the tests, from your earlier Sidekick pieces: `TaskItem` (Id, Title, EstimateMinutes, LoggedMinutes, Done, IsRunning, Tag, Project, Due), `TimeEntry(int TaskId, DateTime Start, DateTime End)` with `Minutes` and `Day`, and `Sk.FormatMinutes`.
starter: static List<string> InvoiceLines(IEnumerable<TaskItem> tasks, IEnumerable<TimeEntry> entries, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, decimal> hourlyRates)
solution: static List<string> InvoiceLines(IEnumerable<TaskItem> tasks, IEnumerable<TimeEntry> entries, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, decimal> hourlyRates)
join t in tasks on e.TaskId equals t.Id
group e.Minutes by t.Project ?? "(no project)" into g
join r in hourlyRates on p.Project equals r.Key into rates
template: var dojoTasks = new List<TaskItem> { new(1, "Fix login") { Project = "web" }, new(2, "Parser") { Project = "core" }, new(3, "Inbox zero"), new(4, "Logo") { Project = "web" } };
DateTime DojoAt(int h, int m) => new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, h, m, 0);
new(1, DojoAt(9, 0), DojoAt(10, 30)), new(4, DojoAt(11, 0), DojoAt(11, 30)), new(2, DojoAt(13, 0), DojoAt(14, 0)),
new(3, DojoAt(15, 0), DojoAt(15, 45)), new(9, DojoAt(16, 0), DojoAt(17, 0)),
Dojo.Eq("one line per project with time, rate or not", 3, dojoLines.Count);
Dojo.Check("web: 2h of time at 80", dojoLines.Contains("web              2h 00m      160.00"), string.Join(" | ", dojoLines));
Dojo.Check("no project, no rate: still listed", dojoLines.Contains("(no project)     0h 45m  unbilled (no rate)"), string.Join(" | ", dojoLines));
Dojo.Eq("a rate with no time adds no line", false, dojoLines.Any(l => l.StartsWith("ops")));
Dojo.Eq("no rates at all: everything unbilled", 3, InvoiceLines(dojoTasks, dojoEntries, new Dictionary<string, decimal>()).Count(l => l.EndsWith("unbilled (no rate)")));
Dojo.Eq("half an hour at 90 is 45.00", new List<string> { "x                0h 30m       45.00" },
InvoiceLines(new List<TaskItem> { new(1, "t") { Project = "x" } }, new List<TimeEntry> { new(1, DojoAt(9, 0), DojoAt(9, 30)) }, new Dictionary<string, decimal> { ["x"] = 90m }));
public TaskItem(int id, string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)
if (id < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(id), "Task ids start at 1.");
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title)) throw new ArgumentException("A task needs a title.", nameof(title));
if (estimateMinutes < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(estimateMinutes), "An estimate cannot be negative.");
public int LoggedMinutes { get; private set; }
public bool IsRunning { get; private set; }
public DateTime StartedAt { get; private set; }
public bool Done { get; private set; }
string projectPart = Project is { Length: > 0 } p ? $" @{p}" : "";
string duePart = Due is DateOnly d ? $" (due {d:ddd d MMM})" : "";
if (Done) throw new InvalidOperationException("A finished task cannot be started.");
if (at < StartedAt) throw new ArgumentException("A timer cannot stop before it started.", nameof(at));
if (minutes < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(minutes), "Log at least one minute.");
enum Status { Todo, Doing, Blocked, Done }
record TimeEntry(int TaskId, DateTime Start, DateTime End)
public static bool CanMove(Status from, Status to) => (from, to) switch
(Status.Doing, Status.Todo or Status.Blocked or Status.Done) => true,
hints: First query: `from e in entries join t in tasks on e.TaskId equals t.Id group e.Minutes by t.Project ?? "(no project)" into g select (Project: g.Key, Minutes: g.Sum())`.
Second query: `from p in perProject join r in hourlyRates on p.Project equals r.Key into rates from rate in rates.DefaultIfEmpty() orderby p.Project select ...`.
No match means `rate.Key is null`. The amount is `p.Minutes / 60m * rate.Value`, formatted `{amount,10:0.00}`.
steps.explain: Two kinds of join in one report: the inner join drops entries of deleted tasks (you cannot bill what you cannot name), and the left join keeps projects you forgot to give a rate, so they are visible instead of silently missing.
